summary: Wilhelm Printz was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Leipzig, Göttingen, Humboldt University of Berlin, and Frankfurt. He served as a librarian for the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft and as an associate professor at the University of Halle-Wittenberg from 1929 to 1939.

Wilhelm Rau worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig and Marburg, earning his PhD under Johannes Nobel. Rau was a professor at Frankfurt in 1955 and served as Ordinarius at Marburg from 1957 to 1988.

Wilhelm Scherer worked in linguistics and related fields. He earned his PhD at Vienna and studied at Berlin under Haupt, Bopp, and Ranke. His posts included chair at Vienna, full professor at Strasbourg, and professor at Berlin from 1877.

Wilhelm Schmidt was a linguist and religious studies scholar who studied in Berlin and Vienna. He directed the Anthropos Institute and served as professor of ethnology at Vienna (1925–1938) and professor at the University of Fribourg from 1939.

Wilhelm Schott specialized in Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Giessen, Berlin, and Halle, where he earned his PhD. He was a Privatdozent at Halle and Berlin, then apl. Professor at Berlin (1838–1884).

Wilhelm Schulze was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Berlin and Greifswald, where he earned his doctorate. He held chairs at the University of Göttingen from 1895 and Humboldt University of Berlin from 1902 to 1932.

Wilhelm Siegling was a scholar of Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He earned his PhD at Humboldt University of Berlin under Richard Pischel and worked at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin and the Prussian Academy of Sciences.
Wilhelm Solf was an Indologist who studied at Berlin, Kiel, Göttingen, Halle (PhD under Richard Pischel), and Jena (Dr.iuris). He held an academic post at Kiel University from ~1888 to 1889.

Wilhelm Storck worked in linguistics and related fields. He studied at Munich, Münster, Bonn, and Humboldt University of Berlin, completing his PhD under Franz Bopp. In 1862, he became an associate professor of German language and literature at Münster.

Wilhelm Streitberg was a linguist and Indologist. He earned a doctorate at Leipzig and completed his habilitation at Münster. He held professorships at Fribourg (1889–1898), Münster (1899–1909), Munich (1909–1920), and Leipzig (1920–1925).

Wilhelm Tomaschek worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, history and archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Vienna under Friedrich Müller and Franz Xaver Miklosich, later becoming professor of geography at Graz and historical geography at Vienna.

Wilhelm Vatke specialized in religious studies and philosophy. He studied at Halle-Wittenberg, Göttingen, and Humboldt University of Berlin, where he subsequently held an academic post from circa 1834 to 1882.

Wilhelm Volck was a scholar of religious studies, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Erlangen-Nuremberg and Leipzig, and served as professor of Semitic Philology at Tartu (1864–1898) and professor at Rostock.

Wilhelm Wackernagel worked in linguistics and related fields. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin under Karl Lachmann and August Boeckh. He held a professorship at the University of Basel from 1833, serving as Ordinarius from 1835 until 1869.

Wilhelm Wissmann was a linguist who earned his PhD at Humboldt University of Berlin under Wilhelm Schulze. He held academic posts at Berlin, the University of Freiburg, the University of Königsberg, and the University of Munich.

Wilhelm Wundt worked in philosophy and other fields. He studied at the universities of Tübingen, Heidelberg, and Berlin, and held posts at the University of Zurich in 1857, the University of Leipzig in 1858, and Heidelberg University in 1864.

Wilhelm von Humboldt worked in linguistics, Indology, and philosophy. He studied at Viadrina, Göttingen, and Jena under teachers including Lichtenberg and Heyne. He served as a Prussian minister in 1819 and held a post at Humboldt University of Berlin.
Wilhelm von Pochhammer was a scholar in the fields of history, archaeology, and Indology. He completed studies at the universities of Freiburg, Marburg, Munich, and Bonn.
Will Sweetman is a scholar of religious studies and Indology. He studied at the University of Cambridge and Lancaster University, and became a professor at the University of Otago circa 2005.

Will Tuladhar-Douglas works in religious and Buddhist studies. He studied at Oxford, including Wolfson College. His posts include lecturer at Aberdeen, director of the Scottish Centre for Himalayan Research, and research fellow at Hamburg.
